*This guide accompanies [the presentation](llms-to-agents.qmd). Each
section names the slide by its title and stable ID, states what the
slide is for, gives an estimated speaking time and a running total, and
then says, in ordinary spoken paragraphs, what to explain and how to use
the visual. Timings are estimates for a 38-minute talk inside a 45-minute
slot, not a rehearsed measurement. The slides' speaker notes carry only
short cues; this page is the script.*

## Running late {#running-late}

Protect the ending. The tools and agents block (slides 21 to 23) is the
part the audience cannot reconstruct from general reading, so shorten
earlier material first. In order, drop or compress: the spoken cat-and-dog
example on the tokens slide (say only that IDs are addresses); the Bengio
2003 sentence on the recurrence slide; the third statement on the base-model
slide; the analogy on the post-training slide; and the "cached" sentence
on the inference slide. If ten minutes have gone before the corpus slide,
skip the product slide and say its one sentence on the runnable-model
slide instead. Never skip the tool-call slide, the agent-loop slide, or
the coding-agent slide.

## From LLMs to Agents {#title-slide}

**Objective:** open the room and set the register. **Time:** about 0.5
min (running total 0.5).

Say who you are in one sentence and what the next forty minutes are: a
mechanical account of what a system like ChatGPT is, how it was built,
and what happens when you type into it, with no mathematics required to
follow and a website that carries the mathematics for anyone who wants
it.

Transition: "Start with the question the whole talk answers."

## One question: what is on the other side of the text box? {#question}

**Objective:** state the governing question and show the whole route
once, in colour, before any term is defined. **Time:** about 1.5 min
(running total 2.0).

Read the question aloud. Then trace the coloured route on the slide from
left to right without explaining any stage yet: blue is data, orange is
training, purple is the model itself, green is the context the model is
given when it is used, and grey is the software around the model. Say
that every slide from here on is one stop on this route, and that the
audience will see the same picture again at the end.

Make one point now, because it organises everything: the orange stages,
pretraining and post-training, are both training. Both change the numbers
inside the model. Everything after the purple "post-trained model" leaves
those numbers alone; it changes what the model is given and what is done
with its output.

Transition: "Here is the route in ordinary words."

Deeper: [The Short Story](../short-story.qmd).

## The route, in three parts {#route}

**Objective:** give the audience three questions to hold. **Time:** about
1.0 min (running total 3.0).

Read the three columns as three questions. How is a model built: text is
prepared, cut into tokens, fed to a neural network, and training sets the
network's numbers. What happens when we use it: your text becomes the
model's context, it produces one token at a time, and its numbers stay
fixed. How does software make an agentic system: tools, stored state, and
a loop around the same fixed model. Promise, explicitly, that the third
question gets real time at the end and will not be rushed.

Transition: "Before any of that, what is the finished object? Start at the
end."

## A runnable model is code plus learned parameters {#runnable-model}

**Objective:** make the finished object concrete before describing the
process that produces it. **Time:** about 2.0 min (running total 5.0).

Point at the two top boxes. Stripped of the product around it, a runnable
open language model is two things. On the left, code: a program that says
how to compute, which sums to form, which nonlinear functions to apply,
which attention steps to take. On the right, a checkpoint: a large file
of learned numbers, the parameters. Andrej Karpathy's 2023 introduction
opens with exactly this picture, using an open model as its example, and
his `llama2.c` repository shows it literally: one C file that runs the
Llama 2 architecture, which cannot generate anything until you give it a
model checkpoint.

Then the bottom box. Running the code with the parameters fixed, on some
context, produces a probability distribution over the next token. That is
inference, and it does not change the parameters. So the talk now has two
halves: how the parameters get their values, and what the surrounding
software does with the object once they have them.

Do not say the file count is always two, and do not say the parameters
are "everything the model knows". Say that the information the model
learned during training is distributed across those numbers.

Transition: "That is the model. The thing you type into is more than the
model."

Deeper: [How Pretraining Works](../learn/training.qmd) §8; Karpathy,
*Intro to Large Language Models* (2023); the `llama2.c` README.

## A ChatGPT-like product is more than the model {#product}

**Objective:** separate the model from the product built around it.
**Time:** about 1.0 min (running total 6.0).

Point at the purple box in the middle: that is the model, the code plus
parameters from the previous slide. Everything else in the grey product
box is either green, meaning context that will be supplied to the model
when it is called (a system prompt, the conversation, files), or grey,
meaning software that acts around the model (retrieval, tools, safety
checks, the interface). Two products can share the same model and behave
differently, and a product can change tomorrow with no training run in
between. Keep this distinction in your pocket; the last third of the talk
lives in the grey box.

Transition: "Now the first half: how the model is built. It starts with
text."

Deeper: [Post-training](../learn/posttraining.qmd) §9.

## Before training, someone builds the corpus {#corpus}

**Objective:** replace "trained on the internet" with a pipeline.
**Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 7.5).

Walk the chips left to right. Text is gathered from web pages, code,
books, and other permitted sources. The main text is extracted from raw
pages, which means stripping menus and markup. Documents are filtered by
language and by quality rules. Duplicates are removed, because a page
copied a thousand times would otherwise be learned a thousand times. Only
then is the surviving text tokenized. Every step is a choice, and what
goes in shapes what can be learned.

Give the one open example: Hugging Face's FineWeb is built from Common
Crawl snapshots by exactly this kind of pipeline, and its recipe is
published. Then the caution: complete corpora for closed models are often
not disclosed, and the level of disclosure varies. Do not imply that
proprietary models use FineWeb, and do not say any model trains on "the
whole internet".

Transition: "The corpus is text. A network computes with numbers. So the
text has to be converted."

Deeper: [From Text to Numbers](../learn/how-created.qmd) §1; Penedo et
al., *The FineWeb Datasets* (2024).

## Text becomes tokens; a token ID is an address {#tokens}

**Objective:** define token and token ID, and kill the idea that an ID
is a quantity. **Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 9.0).

Point at the chips. The tokenizer cuts text into entries of a fixed
vocabulary decided before training. A token is often a whole word, but it
can be a fragment, a punctuation mark, or a word with its leading space
attached; the split shown is illustrative, and different models split
differently. Each vocabulary entry has an index, the token ID. The numbers
on the slide are made up.

Then the point that matters: 5109 is not larger, later, or more than 88.
It does not sit "101 units away" from anything. It only says which entry
of the vocabulary this is. If the network did arithmetic on the ID itself,
the result would be meaningless. So it does not, which raises the
question the next slide answers.

Transition: "If the ID is only an address, what does the network actually
compute with?"

Deeper: [From Text to Numbers](../learn/how-created.qmd) §3–§4; Radford
et al. (2019) for the tokenizer facts.

## The ID selects a learned vector {#embeddings}

**Objective:** explain why an ID becomes a vector, and what "learned"
means here. **Time:** about 1.0 min (running total 10.0).

Trace the figure. The token "bank" becomes ID 3912. The ID selects one
row of a table, the embedding table. That row is a list of numbers, and
those numbers are parameters: they started arbitrary, and training
changed them because changing them improved next-token prediction. By the
end of training, tokens that occur in similar contexts tend to have
similar rows. That is what the lookup buys the network: instead of an
address, it receives numbers it can transform and combine. The values on
the slide are illustrative; a row is not a definition.

Add the one sentence that prepares the transformer: the row is only the
starting point. Later layers of the network update each position using
the positions around it, so " bank" starts the same in "river bank" and
"central bank" and ends different.

Transition: "Numbers going into a network. What does the network do with
them?"

Deeper: [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](../learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§6–§7; Bengio et al. (2003).

## A neural network: learned transformations and nonlinear steps {#neural-network}

**Objective:** make "neural network" mean something mechanical.
**Time:** about 1.0 min (running total 11.0).

Walk the four boxes. Incoming numbers, x. Multiply them by learned
weights and add a learned bias: that is the box Wx + b, and W and b are
parameters. Apply a fixed nonlinear function, sigma, to the result. Out
comes h, a new list of numbers, ready to be the input of the next piece.
If you read the formula aloud, read it as those four steps and say plainly
that this is not "the equation for ChatGPT"; it is the smallest piece from
which large networks are built. Large networks stack millions of these
pieces in layers, and training sets the weights.

Transition: "Networks like this were predicting language long before
transformers."

Deeper: [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](../learn/neural-networks.qmd),
which works one unit through by hand.

## Neural language models came first; recurrence paid a price {#recurrence}

**Objective:** place transformers in history and state the recurrent
constraint mechanically. **Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 12.5).

First the history, in one breath: a 2003 model already learned a vector
for each word together with a network that predicted the next word.
Transformers are not the beginning of neural networks or of neural
language models.

Then the figure. For sequences, recurrent networks, including LSTMs,
became the established approach. They read one position at a time and
pass a running state forward. So information from token 1 reaches token
5 only through four sequential steps, and each step's computation depends
on the previous one having finished. That has two costs: a long path
between distant positions, and, during training, no way to compute the
positions in parallel. Do not say "recurrent networks could not remember";
say the path was long and the computation was sequential.

Transition: "Attention is the mechanism that gave positions a direct
path."

Deeper: [Why Transformers](../learn/why-transformers.qmd) §1–§2; Vaswani
et al. (2017) §1 for the sequential-dependency statement.

## Attention: each position combines what it is allowed to see {#attention}

**Objective:** explain what attention computes before the Transformer
paper is named. **Time:** about 2.0 min (running total 14.5).

Point at "it", the destination. The sentence on the slide is "The
bridge closed because it", shortened so that every token fits at
projection size. For each source position that "it" is permitted to use,
the model computes a weight from learned transformations of the vectors
involved. The weights on the slide are illustrative, and they sum to one;
here "bridge" gets most of the weight and "because" the next largest
share.
The model then takes the weighted combination of the sources' vectors and
uses it to update the representation of "it". That is the whole
mechanism: a learned, weighted mixing of other positions, in one step,
with no relay through the positions in between.

Two guard rails. First, the weights are not written by anyone; they come
out of matrices that training set. Second, a weight is a local mixing
number inside one head at one layer. Real models run many heads in
parallel and stack many layers, so no single weight tells you why the
model said what it said.

Attention came before the Transformer: Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio used a
learned weighted selection of this kind for translation in work posted in
2014 and presented at ICLR 2015.

Transition: "In 2017 one paper built the whole architecture around this
mechanism."

Deeper: [How Self-Attention Moves Information](../learn/transformers-attention.qmd);
Vaswani et al. (2017) §3.2; Bahdanau et al. (2015).

Do not imply: that an attention weight is a probability that one token
caused another, or that one head has a fixed human-readable job.

## The Transformer: attention plus feed-forward, without recurrence {#transformer}

**Objective:** name the paper, state what it changed, and keep training
parallelism distinct from generation. **Time:** about 1.5 min (running
total 16.0).

Name it: *Attention Is All You Need*, Vaswani and colleagues, 2017. At a
time when recurrent networks were the established state of the art, it
built a sequence architecture around two computations per block:
attention, which moves information between positions, and a feed-forward
step, which is the network piece from the earlier slide applied to each
position on its own. No recurrence. Point at the arcs: in one layer, any
position can read any permitted earlier position directly.

Then the precision that matters. During training on a known sequence,
the positions within a layer can be computed in parallel, because nothing
waits for a previous position to finish. Generation is different: at use
time the model still produces one token at a time. And the model is
causal: a position never sees later tokens.

On hardware, keep it restrained: parallel computation over matrices fits
GPUs and later accelerators well, and that fit was one reason among
several for the architecture's spread, alongside scale, data, and the
software around it. Dense attention also has a cost that grows with the
square of the sequence length.

Transition: "Now the numbers get their values. Pretraining."

Deeper: [Why Transformers](../learn/why-transformers.qmd) §3–§6.

Do not imply: that attention alone is the Transformer, or that GPU
compatibility is the whole explanation.

## Pretraining: the text supplies its own answers {#pretraining}

**Objective:** state the training loop with the three jobs kept apart.
**Time:** about 2.0 min (running total 18.0).

Walk the chips. Token sequences from the corpus go in. At every position
the model predicts the next token, and the text itself supplies the
answer, because the next token is right there; no one labels anything. A
loss measures how little probability the model gave to the token that
actually came next. Backpropagation computes, for the trainable
parameters, how the loss would change with a small change in them: the
gradients. The optimizer uses those gradients to change the parameters by
a small step. Then the next batch, and the next, on a scale that is hard
to picture.

Say the three jobs explicitly, because they get confused: the loss
measures, backpropagation computes gradients, the optimizer updates. The
architecture and the optimization procedure are specified in code;
training is the process that discovers the parameter values. The result
is the base model.

Transition: "What is a base model, and what is it not?"

Deeper: [How Pretraining Works](../learn/training.qmd) §1–§5.

## The base model is not a database and not yet an assistant {#base-model}

**Objective:** prevent two misreadings of the base model. **Time:** about
1.0 min (running total 19.0).

Three statements, one each. Because predicting text well requires
capturing its regularities, the base model has broad statistical
knowledge of grammar, meaning, recurring facts, and conventions of
argument; models trained only to predict text have been observed to
answer questions and translate without being trained for those tasks.
Second, it can reproduce text it saw, but it stores no verified,
searchable record of the corpus; a fact appears in its output only
because predicting the text made reproducing that fact useful, and
nothing in the objective checks truth. Third, it is not specifically
optimized to behave as an assistant: given an instruction, it may answer
it, continue it, or produce more instructions like it, because all of
those follow such text somewhere in the corpus.

Transition: "Turning that into an assistant is more training, on the same
numbers."

Deeper: [How Pretraining Works](../learn/training.qmd) §6–§7.

Do not imply: that the model cannot memorize or reproduce training text,
or that it is a database you can query.

## Post-training changes the same parameters with different data {#post-training}

**Objective:** establish post-training as training, and name the three
routes. **Time:** about 2.5 min (running total 21.5).

Point at the three cards and say the invariant first: every card is the
same loss-gradient-optimizer machinery changing the same parameter
collection. What differs is the data and the objective. No new kind of
network appears.

Card one is pretraining, already covered. Card two is supervised
fine-tuning: curated conversations, a prompt and the response the
builders want, trained with the same next-token loss on the response
tokens, so that after training a request is treated as a request. Card
three is a family: preference-based methods compare candidate responses
and update the parameters toward the preferred one, either through a
learned reward model and reinforcement learning, the route usually called
RLHF, or directly from the comparison pairs; and reward-based methods use
outcomes that can be scored. The influential 2022 recipe used
human-written demonstrations and human comparisons; published recipes
since also use model-generated data and feedback from models, rules, or
automatic checks. Providers combine and vary all of this.

Optional, if time allows, and labelled as an analogy: Karpathy organises
these stages as reading exposition, studying worked examples, and doing
practice problems against an answer key. It explains why later stages use
more targeted data, and it is not a claim that models learn as people do.

Close with the one thing that is not post-training: a product's system
prompt is text in the context and changes nothing in the model.

Transition: "So why can a fluent assistant still be wrong?"

Deeper: [Post-training](../learn/posttraining.qmd) §2–§6; Ouyang et al.
(2022); Rafailov et al. (2023).

Do not imply: that RLHF is a synonym for post-training, or that all
post-training data is written by human labelers.

## Why a fluent answer can still be wrong {#fluency}

**Objective:** give the correct causal story for unsupported answers.
**Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 23.0).

Three statements. Pretraining rewards assigning probability to whatever
came next in the text; nothing in it checks truth, so false or
unsupported continuations are possible before any post-training.
Post-training then makes instruction-following and question-answering
the default, so a well-formed answer can outrun what the parameters
actually contain; post-training did not create the possibility of
unsupported answers, it changed the default form of the response.
Finally, the remedies: recipes can teach abstention, so that "I don't
know" becomes a likely response when knowledge is thin; and retrieval and
tools can ground an answer in inspectable evidence placed in the context.
That evidence still has to be evaluated, because retrieval can return
irrelevant or wrong material.

The sentence to leave in the room: fluency is not evidence.

Transition: "One more kind of training, because it is easy to
misdescribe."

Deeper: [How Pretraining Works](../learn/training.qmd) §7;
[Using Models Well](../learn/using-models-well.qmd) §4–§6.

Do not imply: that post-training caused hallucination, or that a retrieved
document makes an answer automatically true.

## Some models are trained to reason longer on checkable problems {#reasoning-training}

**Objective:** describe reasoning-oriented training as one route.
**Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 24.5).

Some problems have outcomes that can be checked automatically: a
mathematics problem with a known answer, code with tests. A checkable
outcome can supply a reward without a learned reward model for that
component, and reinforcement learning against such rewards can encourage
useful intermediate reasoning before the final answer. The published case
is DeepSeek-R1. Keep its two models apart: R1-Zero applied
reinforcement learning directly to the already pretrained base model,
with no supervised fine-tuning step first, and it produced steadily
longer reasoning traces but suffered from poor readability and language
mixing; the released R1 used a multi-stage recipe that also included
supervised stages. This is one route used by some reasoning-oriented models, not a
stage every model passes through, and other providers publish less.

Transition: "That is training. 'Thinking longer' also means something at
use time."

Deeper: [Post-training](../learn/posttraining.qmd) §7; DeepSeek-AI
(2025).

## "Thinking longer" at inference spends computation, not training {#thinking-longer}

**Objective:** explain inference-time reasoning mechanically and with its
limits. **Time:** about 2.0 min (running total 26.5).

Point at the three rows. Row one: prompt in, answer out. Row two: the
same model, with the same fixed parameters, generates intermediate
reasoning tokens before its answer. Each intermediate token becomes part
of the context that the next step conditions on, so the model gets more
sequential computation before it commits. Nothing was retrained; the
next-token mechanism did not go away. Row three: the reasoning can produce
a tool request, software runs the tool, the observation comes back into
the context, and reasoning continues with new evidence. Hold that row; it
returns in a few slides.

Then the limits. Providers expose this differently, as effort levels or
thinking levels, and what you see of the reasoning depends on the
product: the three providers whose documentation the course cites return
a summary rather than the raw tokens, and Anthropic's own announcement
says the visible thought process is not guaranteed to represent what is
going on inside the model.
More reasoning is not a guarantee of a correct answer. And generated
reasoning is output from the same mechanism as any other output, not
thought in the human sense.

Transition: "The model is built. Now the second half: what happens when
you type."

Deeper: [Post-training](../learn/posttraining.qmd) §7; Anthropic, Google,
and OpenAI reasoning documentation, accessed 2026-09-15.

Do not imply: that a displayed reasoning summary is a faithful account of
every internal computation, or that all providers implement this the same
way.

## What happens when you type {#inference-loop}

**Objective:** follow one request through the loop. **Time:** about 2.0
min (running total 28.5).

Trace the figure. The product assembles and manages the context: its
system prompt, the conversation so far, any documents or tool results it
includes, and your message. The tokenizer turns that text into token IDs.
Each ID selects its embedding. The transformer blocks update every
position. The final position's vector becomes one score per vocabulary
entry, the logits. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities. A decoding
rule selects one token, deterministically or at random from the
distribution. That token is appended to the context, and the loop runs
again. A paragraph of output is this loop, one token at a time.

Two sentences to close. Nothing in the parameters changes; the system
prompt and supplied documents are context, not retraining. And, briefly,
implementations cache the keys and values already computed for earlier
positions rather than recomputing them each step.

Transition: "Three different places can carry information for the model.
Keeping them apart explains most product behaviour."

Deeper: [Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature](../learn/softmax-sampling.qmd);
[How Pretraining Works](../learn/training.qmd) §9.

## Parameters, context, and external state are different places {#three-stores}

**Objective:** separate the three stores. **Time:** about 1.5 min
(running total 30.0).

Left box: parameters, inside the model, changed only by training. Middle
box: the context, the tokens supplied for this step, assembled or managed
by the product. Right box: external state, files, databases, saved notes,
kept by software outside the model and retrievable into a later context.
Only the first is the model changing. A product that "remembers" your
project across sessions stored something outside the model and supplied
it again; no parameter was updated. All three get called "memory", which
is why the word confuses people.

Optional and labelled as an analogy: Karpathy calls the context the
model's working memory. The course extends that to parametric knowledge
as imperfect long-term recall and explicit context as what is in front
of the system right now. It is an intuition about why supplying a
document works, not a claim about the network's anatomy.

Transition: "Now the grey box from the start: tools. One concrete
example."

Deeper: [From Assistant to Agent](../learn/agents.qmd) §7;
[Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](../learn/tokens-context.qmd) §8–§10.

## One tool call: the model asks, software acts {#tool-call}

**Objective:** teach tool use with one round trip. **Time:** about 2.0
min (running total 32.0).

Set the scene: someone asks, "What is the weather in Bogotá today?" The
parameters cannot contain today's weather, and a model call by itself
does not read files, run programs, or search anything. Then walk the six
cards. One, the context holds the request and a description of a weather
tool: its name, what it does, the inputs it takes. Two, instead of
inventing a value, the model generates structured output that means
"call weather with location Bogotá"; that is generated text in a
structured format, nothing more. Three, the surrounding software
recognises the request, checks its permission rules, and runs the tool.
Four, the tool returns a result; the value on the slide is invented for
the example. Five, the software places the result into the model's next
context. Six, the model generates the answer, now resting on the result.

The boundary, said plainly: the model requested the action; software
executed it; the result became new context. Purple cards are model
output; grey cards are execution outside the model.

Transition: "Repeat that round trip under control, and you have an
agentic system."

Deeper: [From Assistant to Agent](../learn/agents.qmd) §2–§3; Anthropic,
*Tool use with Claude* documentation.

Do not imply: that the model itself ran the tool, or that the example
weather is real.

## Repeat the round trip under control: an agentic system {#agent-loop}

**Objective:** define the loop and the workflow-versus-agent distinction.
**Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 33.5).

Walk the chips as a loop. An objective, the current context, and the
current state go to the model. The model returns a tool request or a
response. A request is checked against permission rules and executed. The
observation goes into the context. The model is called again, and the
loop continues, asks the user, or stops. The model does not run between
calls; software carries the state.

Then the vocabulary, briefly. In a workflow, the sequence of steps is
written in advance and the model fills in each step. In an agent, the
model chooses which steps and tools to use, within limits set by the
software. Neither is better in general, the simplest system that reliably
solves the task is usually the right one, and the terminology is not
standardised. Either way, an agent is a control pattern around the same
fixed model, not a new architecture.

Transition: "One agent you may meet this year: a coding agent."

Deeper: [From Assistant to Agent](../learn/agents.qmd) §4–§6; Anthropic,
*Building effective agents* (2024).

Do not imply: that "agent" means fully autonomous, or that a new neural
network appears at this stage.

## A coding agent: inspect, edit, run checks, revise, stop {#coding-agent}

**Objective:** make the loop concrete and end with verification and
permissions. **Time:** about 2.0 min (running total 35.5).

Walk the chips with a story. A user says, "find why this script fails
and fix it." The agent requests a listing of the files and the failing
script's output; the software runs those and returns the traceback. The
model reads it, requests one file, and proposes an edit; the software
asks for approval, then applies it. The model requests the tests; the
software runs them and returns the output. If a test still fails, the
loop continues from the evidence; if the specified checks pass, it reports
and stops.

Three closing points. Project instructions and skills are context loaded
for the task; they are files read into the context, not retraining.
Permissions live in the software: what runs automatically, what waits for
approval, what is refused. And a passing test establishes only what that
test checked; whether the right thing was built remains a human judgment.
Claude Code is one current example of such a system; the mechanism is
general.

Transition: "That is the whole route. One picture to keep."

Deeper: [From Assistant to Agent](../learn/agents.qmd) §8–§11; Claude
Code documentation, accessed 2026-09-15.

Do not imply: that "done" in an agent's output is evidence, or that giving
an agent a skill retrains it.

## The mental model {#mental-model}

**Objective:** compress the talk into one statement and four
consequences. **Time:** about 1.5 min (running total 37.0).

Say it slowly. A language model is a learned next-token predictor: code
plus parameters, set by pretraining and post-training. Once trained, the
parameters are fixed; what is specific to a request arrives through the
context. Software adds tools, state, and a loop, and that loop of model
step, action, and evidence is what turns a predictor into a system that
carries out work.

Then the four consequences, one breath each. Fluency is not evidence.
Tool use is not automatically verification. A passing check proves only
what it tested. On judgment-heavy questions, evidence, review, and
accountability stay with people.

Transition: "Everything here is on the website, with the mathematics and
the sources."

Deeper: [Using Models Well](../learn/using-models-well.qmd).

## Where to learn more {#learn-more}

**Objective:** send people to the right next page. **Time:** about 1.0
min (running total 38.0).

Point to the Short Story first: the same route as this talk, with the
mathematics, in about twenty minutes. Then the seven main-path lessons in
order, the glossary for any term used today, the milestones page for the
history, and the resources page, which begins with a video-first route
for people who would rather watch than read. Every factual claim on the
